sentences.text: The seal came up six feet off the port bow and looked at her.
Maeve stopped rowing.
She was grey and she was enormous — much bigger than Maeve had pictured, and she had pictured her often — and she had a scar across the bridge of her nose that had gone pale.
The water ran off the top of her head.

She was low in the water, only the head and a little of the shoulder, and she was completely still, and she looked at Maeve with round black eyes that were not kind and not unkind and not anything, and were paying complete attention.
They stayed like that for a length of time that Maeve has never been able to estimate.
She has said thirty seconds.
She has said four minutes.
She does not know.
Nothing happened.
That is the part she has never been able to explain to anybody, including herself.
There was no sign.
Nothing was communicated.
The seal did not nod, or gesture, or swim in a meaningful direction, or do any of the things that would have made it a story with a shape.

She looked at Maeve, in the flat grey light, with the oars up and the water ticking under the hull, until Maeve understood that she was being looked at properly — the way almost nobody looks at an eleven year old — and then she went down without a splash and did not come up again.
Maeve sat in the punt for a while.
Then she rowed in, and tied up, and carried the empty box up the steps, and went home, and had her dinner, and did not say the sentence.
She has never worked out what happened.
She has considered every version of it.
That the seal comes to stop you.
That the seal comes because you are about to stop and the stopping is the thing that calls her, and she has no opinion about it whatsoever, and just comes to look, the way you look at a fire.
That there is no seal and there is only an ordinary grey seal in an ordinary bay and seven people over sixty years happening to be at the end of their rope on the day they saw her.
She thinks the last one is probably true and she does not think it makes any difference.

Because the thing that actually happened, the thing she can point to, was this: for four minutes on a Tuesday in July, at the exact moment when she had decided that what she was doing did not count, something came up out of the water and gave her its whole attention.
She kept the creels going until September, when the season ended, which was always when it was going to end.
Her grandmother died the following March.
The creels went to the Coyles, which is what her grandmother had arranged in February without telling anybody, because she was that sort of woman.
Maeve is twenty-six now and she has not seen the seal again, and she does not expect to, and she has never once gone looking.
She did tell her father, in the end.
Not that summer — years later, in the van, going to Sligo for something else.
He drove for about a mile without saying anything.
Then he said: "Where was she?" "Just off the black buoy." "Mm," her father said.
"That's where she was for me." And he put the radio on, and they went on to Sligo, and that is the only conversation the two of them have ever had about it.
